catalog_quote: From a lexical standpoint, the tone systems found in the Lower Cross languages are relatively straightforward: in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D) which operates on H tones. In many cases, comparative evidence shows downstep to be related to diachronic developments, and as such, at least in these cases, can be analysed as a floating L between two Hs. Combinations of two tones on one syllable may occur, to give HL—i.e., a falling tone—or LH, a rising tone. ... From a phrasal perspective, the Lower Cross languages are of the classic terracing type; i.e., each instance of D within a phrase lowers the ceiling on H tones within that phrase, with the ceiling being reset at the beginning of each subsequent phrase. new_statements.rule_in_words: Oro, like every Lower Cross language, is a terraced-level tone language with lexical H and L plus contrastive downstep (and HL/LH contours on single syllables); no word-stress rule is given -- the only mention of stress is an uninvestigated interaction of tone with phrase-level stress. Simmons 1965 (Oro-specific, p.33) independently describes nouns as carrying low, mid, high, falling and rising tones and likewise says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Connell notes falling tones from tone spreading are dialect/language-specific within the group; Simmons 1965 records a marginal mid tone and interrogative/vocative tone changes in Oro.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement covering all Lower Cross languages, Oro explicitly included (Connell collected first-hand Lower Cross data incl. Oro); lexical tone described at word level, stress mentioned only at phrase level and as uninvestigated. No source opened states where word stress falls in Oro.
new_statements.identity_note: Connell 1994's tone statement is framed for the whole Lower Cross group (Oro = Oron, ~400,000 speakers with some dialect variation, explicitly among the languages surveyed, glottocode oroo1241); Simmons's Oro-specific data (1956/1960/1965) come from a single speaker of Eweme village recorded in 1953. 'Oron' (Simmons) and 'Oro/Örö/Nsíŋ Oro' are the same language (ISO orx).

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 (p.10): all Lower Cross languages (Oro explicitly among them, p.4) have two tones H and L plus contrastive downstep on H; HL/LH contours; terracing, automatic downstep, downdrift. Sec. 3.4: light/heavy syllables organised into bimoraic feet, equivalent unit posited for Oro as 'syllable piece' (Kuperus 1978). Sec. 5 (p.12): tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress' but uninvestigated except Faraclas 1984b for Obolo. No word-stress placement statement.
